panels.title: Status — is it running, and is it sending?
Mode
panels.description: The single most important fact about a running instance. 1 means every transaction is built, signed and then logged; 0 means it is on the wire.

panels.title: Replication
panels.description: While this is 0 the worker learns about nothing new. Stream positions are stale.

panels.title: Synapse DB role
panels.description: Whether the connection to Synapse's database can write. A primary sender MUST be able to: its cursor is a set of deletions.

panels.title: Destinations known
panels.description: Queues that exist. Grows to this worker's share of the destination list and stops.

panels.title: Backing off
panels.description: Destinations refusing to be dialled. A large number is NORMAL — a homeserver's destination list is mostly a graveyard. Watch its SHAPE: a step change means a problem at our end, not theirs.

panels.title: Version
panels.description: Build stamped at compile time.

panels.title: Throughput
panels.description: What this worker is getting through.

panels.title: Events examined per second
panels.description: Examined counts every event the pickup loop looked at; routed counts those that produced at least one destination in this shard. Most events are remote-origin and are correctly skipped, so the gap between the two lines is expected and large.

panels.title: Transactions per second
panels.description: Transactions this worker put on the wire. One shard's worth: what this worker owns is sha256(destination) mod len(federation_sender_instances).

panels.title: PDUs and EDUs per second
panels.description: Broken down by EDU type, matching Synapse's own synapse_federation_client_sent_edus_by_type_total. The breakdown is what makes the total readable: presence was 99.6% of what the Python senders on this homeserver sent, so a change in the total says almost nothing about whether any particular EDU is being routed at all.

panels.title: Events skipped, by reason
panels.description: Shape matters more than height. 'remote origin' dominating is correct — most traffic is other servers' events. A filter that suddenly rejects everything shows up here as a change in composition, not merely a drop in throughput.

panels.title: Latency
panels.description: How long the work takes, stage by stage.

panels.title: Event processing lag (p50 / p95 / p99)
panels.description: Seconds from an event being persisted to this worker finishing routing it. The headline number for a sender: it is what a user waits for.

panels.title: Where the time goes, per stage (p95)
panels.description:
The panel that says WHERE to optimise, and it has already answered once: the goroutine fan-out this design bets on costs microseconds, while destination resolution costs milliseconds. The bottleneck is the database, not the concurrency model.

Unaffected by replay, unlike the lag panel.

panels.title: Fan-out duration (p50 / p95 / p99)
panels.description: Time to hand one event to every destination queue in this shard. The number the whole design is a bet on.

panels.title: Destinations per routed event
panels.description: The fan-out width -- how many servers one event has to reach. One goroutine each is the bet this worker is built on, so this is the load that bet is taken against.

panels.title: State group cache hit rate
panels.description: The joined-host lookup is the most expensive thing in the per-event path -- a recursive walk of the state group edges, hundreds of milliseconds on a deep chain and seconds at worst. A state group is immutable, so the answer is cached with no invalidation and the query runs once per state CHANGE rather than once per event. Events between two state changes share a group (14.5 of them here, measured), so expect a high rate; a falling one means rooms are changing membership faster than the cache holds them, or that it is too small. 'entries held' against resolution.host_cache_entries answers whether a bigger cache would help: while it sits below the limit nothing has been evicted, so every miss is a first sight of a state group and raising the limit changes nothing.

panels.title: Queued work
panels.description: Sampled rather than tracked by counter, so a leak shows up even when the counters that should have caught it are themselves the buggy part. Steady growth means delivery is not keeping up with routing.

panels.title: Send duration by outcome (p95)
panels.description: Labelled by outcome because a fast failure and a fast success are indistinguishable in a duration histogram — a remote that refuses instantly would otherwise read as excellent performance.

panels.title: Sends in flight
panels.description: Against queue.max_concurrent_destinations. Pinned at the bound means the concurrency limit, not the network, is what is pacing delivery.

panels.title: Replication rows by stream
panels.description: A stream that stops arriving is invisible everywhere else: the worker simply has less to do and looks healthy.

panels.title: Events stream position
panels.description: How far through the events stream this worker has read. A stream ordering of ONE homeserver: it counts that server's events and means nothing next to another deployment's number.

panels.title: Routing accuracy
panels.description: Where this worker had to fall back to current room state instead of the state before the event.

panels.title: Approximate routes, by cause
panels.description:
Routing decisions that fell back to CURRENT room state instead of resolving the state before the event.

'forked dag' is work not done here -- full state resolution is room-sized. It should be rare; a rising line means events are being routed from a state that is close, not exact.

panels.title: Write operations per second
panels.description: A primary sender's bookkeeping: the deletions and cursor writes that ARE its position. A flat zero here while events flow means the sender is not recording what it delivered, and a restart would replay it.

panels.title: Write failures
panels.description: Non-zero here in primary mode means delivery is working while the bookkeeping is not: rows are re-read forever, the outbox grows without bound, and prev_id chaining silently lags. Nothing else reports it.

panels.title: Go runtime — what the concurrency model costs
Goroutines
panels.description: One goroutine per destination with work is the bet this worker is built on, so this is that bet in numbers. Read it against 'destinations with queued work': goroutines should track it, plus a small constant. Wake spawns before taking a concurrency slot, so this can legitimately exceed queue.max_concurrent_destinations -- the excess is goroutines parked waiting for a slot, not sends in flight. A count that climbs while queued work does not is a leak.

panels.title: Memory
panels.description: Resident is what the host sees; heap in-use is what Go is holding. The gap between heap in-use and heap allocated is memory Go has freed but not returned to the OS, so resident lags a drop in real usage by minutes -- expect it after a large queue is dropped rather than reading it as a leak. Stack in-use is roughly the goroutine count times 8-16KB, and is the direct cost of the concurrency model.

panels.title: CPU
panels.description: Cores, not percent: 1 means one core saturated. The claim this worker makes is that a thousand destinations cost goroutines rather than a reactor, so this is the number that has to stay low while transactions per second does not.

panels.title: Open file descriptors
panels.description: One per open connection, so this tracks how many remote servers are being talked to at once. Plotted against the process limit because exhausting it does not look like a resource problem from the outside -- it looks like every destination failing at once, which reads as a network outage.

panels.title: GC pauses and frequency
panels.description: p50 and worst-case stop-the-world pause, with collections per second. A sender holding queues for thousands of destinations gives the collector a large live set to scan; rising pauses here show up as latency everywhere else and nothing else names the cause.
